q: Which gas, released when you chop pyaaz, makes your eyes sting and water?
note: Enzymes make it only once the bulb's cells are cut open.

q: Why does a sharp knife cause fewer tears than a blunt one when chopping pyaaz?
options: It cuts too fast for the gas to rise
note: A blunt blade bursts more cells, releasing more of the irritant.

q: Which pungent compound forms within seconds when lehsun is crushed or chopped?
note: It forms when the enzyme alliinase acts on its odourless precursor, alliin.

q: The nose-tingling kick of freshly ground sarson paste comes from which group of compounds?
note: They form when crushed seeds meet water, which activates the enzyme myrosinase.

q: Why doesn't gulping water put out a chilli burn?
options: Capsaicin reacts with water to form acid
note: Capsaicin dissolves readily in fats and oils instead.

q: Which milk protein binds capsaicin and helps wash away a chilli burn?
note: A Penn State study found skim milk eased the burn as well as whole milk.

q: Capsaicin feels hot because it switches on the nerve receptor that normally detects what?
note: That receptor, TRPV1, normally fires at temperatures above about 43°C.

q: Most of a green chilli's capsaicin is found not in the seeds but in which white part holding them?
note: Seeds taste hot mainly because they touch the capsaicin-rich pith.

q: Which compound gives kali mirch its pungent bite?
note: Black, white and green peppercorns all come from the same climbing vine.

q: Which compound gives fresh adrak its pungency?
note: Drying turns some of it into shogaols, which are even more pungent.

q: Eugenol, used in some dental cements, is the main aroma compound of which spice?
note: Its oil is mostly eugenol, which gives the spice its numbing warmth.

q: Menthol in pudina feels cooling because it triggers nerve receptors that normally sense what?
note: Nothing actually gets colder; the nerve simply reports a chill.

q: Which browning reaction between sugars and amino acids gives toast, dosa crusts and seared paneer their flavour?
note: It is named after the French chemist who described it in 1912.

q: Which enzyme makes cut aloo and baingan slices turn brown in air?
note: It oxidises phenolic compounds, which then form brown pigments called melanins.

q: Why does a squeeze of lemon keep cut fruit from browning?
a: Its acid slows the browning enzyme
options: Its acid slows the browning enzyme
It kills bacteria on the surface
It adds extra water to the cells
It coats the fruit in sugar

q: The browning of cut fruit needs which gas from the air?
note: Keeping cut aloo under water slows browning by cutting off air.

q: Which gas, made by yeast, makes bread dough rise?
note: Yeast gets its energy by breaking down sugars in the flour.

q: Baker's yeast is what kind of living thing?
note: A single gram of dried yeast holds billions of living cells.

q: What genus name, meaning 'sugar fungus' in Greek, do baker's and brewer's yeasts share?
note: The full species name is Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

q: Which stretchy protein network forms when wheat flour is kneaded with water?
note: Kneading lines up its strands so dough can trap gas and hold its shape.

q: Which autoimmune condition is triggered by certain proteins in wheat, barley and rye?
note: It is a different condition from a wheat allergy.

q: Besides the gas that raises dough, yeast also makes which substance that bakes off in the oven?
note: It is part of the aroma of freshly baked bread.

q: Roughly what water temperature kills baker's yeast?
note: Lukewarm water suits it best; very hot water kills it.

q: Letting shaped dough rise before baking is called what?
note: Bakeries often do it in a warm, humid cabinet.

q: What is the final burst of rising a loaf gets in its first minutes in a hot oven called?
note: Expanding gas, water turning to steam and a last yeast spurt all help.

q: Why does a loaf's crust brown while the soft inside stays pale?
a: The moist inside can't get much hotter than 100°C
options: The pan blocks heat from the inside
The moist inside can't get much hotter than 100°C
note: Once the surface dries out, it heats well past boiling point and browns.

q: Bread goes stale mainly because of what?
note: Keeping bread in the fridge actually makes it go stale faster.

q: Curd tastes sour because bacteria turn milk sugar into which acid?
note: The acid also makes milk proteins clump, which thickens the curd.

q: Which rod-shaped bacteria, named after the Latin word for milk, are classic curd-setting microbes?
note: A spoonful of old curd carries these microbes into fresh milk.

q: Why is milk kept lukewarm, not fridge-cold, when setting curd?
a: The bacteria grow fastest when warm
options: Cold milk is too thick to set
The bacteria grow fastest when warm
note: Curd sets much more slowly in winter for the same reason.

q: Kombucha is made by fermenting sweetened what?
note: Microbes turn the sugar into acids and a gentle fizz.

q: What is the rubbery disc of microbes that ferments kombucha usually called?
note: The name stands for Symbiotic Culture Of Bacteria and Yeast.

q: The mould Aspergillus oryzae, used for soy sauce and miso, is known in Japan by what name?
note: Its enzymes break down starch and protein before other microbes take over.

q: To make paneer at home, hot milk is split by adding what?
note: The leftover greenish liquid is called whey.

q: Why does stale milk curdle when you boil it?
options: Its fat has turned to sugar
note: Heat speeds up the clumping that the acid has already started.

q: Why does milk boil over when water doesn't?
a: A skin of proteins traps the steam
options: Fat makes milk expand when hot
A skin of proteins traps the steam
Milk boils at a much lower temperature

q: Which French scientist gave his name to the gentle heating process that makes packaged milk safe?
note: He first used gentle heating to stop wine spoiling, in the 1860s.

q: Standard HTST treatment of milk heats it to about 72°C for how long?
note: HTST stands for High Temperature, Short Time.

q: Why does a pressure cooker whistle?
a: Built-up steam lifts the weight to escape
options: Built-up steam lifts the weight to escape
note: Each whistle releases just enough steam to keep the pressure steady.

q: Which enzyme digests milk sugar, and runs low in people who get stomach upsets from dairy?
note: Many adults around the world make less of it after childhood.

q: Which fatty compound in egg yolk helps oil and water stay blended in sauces?
note: Commercial lecithin is often extracted from soybeans or sunflower seeds.

q: Butter is best described as which kind of mixture?
note: Churning turns one type of emulsion into the other.

q: A homemade egg-and-oil sauce is most likely to 'split' if what happens?
a: The oil is poured in too fast
options: The oil is poured in too fast
A pinch of salt is added
The eggs are at room temperature
note: Adding oil drop by drop lets the yolk coat each new droplet.

q: Which dairy process breaks fat into tiny droplets so it doesn't separate out on top of milk?
note: Milk is forced at high pressure through very narrow gaps.

q: Milk looks white because its tiny fat droplets and protein clusters do what to light?
note: Skimmed milk, with less fat, can look slightly bluish.

q: What is the temperature at which a heated cooking oil starts giving off continuous smoke called?
note: Past it, the oil breaks down and can taste acrid.

q: Which of these can usually be heated the hottest before it starts smoking?
note: Refining strips out particles that would otherwise burn early.

q: Ghee can handle higher heat than butter mainly because what has been removed?
note: Those milk solids brown during the long simmer, giving it a nutty aroma.

q: Why are whole spices sizzled in hot oil for a tadka?
a: Many aroma compounds dissolve in fat
options: Many aroma compounds dissolve in fat
Spices only release colour in oil
note: Once in the fat, the flavour spreads evenly through the whole dal.

q: Partially hydrogenating vegetable oil, as in vanaspati, creates which harmful type of fat?
note: Since January 2022, FSSAI caps industrial trans fat at 2% of the total fat in oils and fats.

q: Fats that stay solid at room temperature, like butter, are mostly which type?
note: Liquid oils are richer in unsaturated fats, whose kinked chains pack loosely.

q: Chips packets are flushed with which gas to stop the oil in the chips oxidising?
note: The puffy cushion of gas also stops the chips from breaking.

q: Does a pinch of salt make a pot of water boil noticeably faster?
a: No, it slightly raises the boiling point
options: No, it stops the water boiling
Yes, salt lowers the boiling point
No, it slightly raises the boiling point
Yes, salt adds heat to the water
note: A pinch shifts the boiling point by only a tiny fraction of a degree.

q: Does searing meat really 'seal in' its juices?
a: No, it adds flavour but seals nothing
options: Yes, but only for thick cuts
Only if it is salted first
Yes, the crust is fully waterproof
No, it adds flavour but seals nothing
note: Tests show seared meat loses as much moisture as unseared meat, or more.

q: Does adding oil to pasta water stop the pasta sticking?
a: No, the oil mostly floats on top
options: No, the oil mostly floats on top
Only if the water is salted
Yes, it lowers the boiling point
note: Plenty of water and stirring early are what actually help.

q: Is the 'five-second rule' for dropped food true?
options: Yes, bacteria need five seconds to move
Yes, but only on tiled floors
note: A 2016 Rutgers study found transfer can begin in under a second.

q: Does eating spicy food cause stomach ulcers?
a: No, most come from bacteria or certain painkillers
options: Only if eaten on an empty stomach
No, most come from bacteria or certain painkillers
Yes, chillies burn holes in the stomach
note: Spicy food may irritate an existing ulcer, but it does not cause one.

q: Water heated undisturbed in a very smooth cup can erupt suddenly. What is this above-boiling state called?
note: The US FDA warns it can cause serious scalds when the cup is moved.

q: Why is rajma soaked overnight before cooking?
a: It absorbs water and cooks faster
options: It absorbs water and cooks faster

q: Raw or undercooked rajma contains which toxic lectin, destroyed by proper boiling?
note: The US FDA warns that slow cookers that stay below boiling may not destroy it.

q: Beans and dal can cause gas because gut bacteria ferment which sugars we can't digest?
note: Humans lack the enzyme alpha-galactosidase needed to break them down.

q: What makes a popcorn kernel burst open when heated?
note: Kernels pop best with roughly 14% moisture inside.

q: What is the hard, moisture-sealing outer skin of a popcorn kernel called?
Popcorn kernels burst when the inside reaches roughly what temperature?
note: Pressure inside builds to about 10 times normal air pressure.

q: The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and which fourth one?
note: The body can store these in fat and the liver.

q: Which of these vitamins is water-soluble?
note: B12 is unusual among them: the liver can store it for years.

q: Which vitamin is most easily lost when vegetables are boiled for a long time?
note: It dissolves in water and breaks down with heat.

q: Polished white rice loses the bran rich in which vitamin, whose lack causes beriberi?
note: Parboiling pushes some of it from the bran into the grain.

q: A lack of which B vitamin causes pellagra?
note: Its symptoms are summed up as the three Ds: dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.

q: One gram of dietary fat provides about how many kilocalories?
note: Carbohydrates and proteins provide about 4 kilocalories per gram.

q: A food 'Calorie' written with a capital C equals how many small calories?
note: So a food Calorie is really a kilocalorie.

q: Which sealed lab device measures a food's energy by completely burning a sample?
note: The heat released warms surrounding water, and that rise is measured.

q: Which plant carbohydrate, a major part of dietary fibre, can human enzymes not digest?
note: Cows and goats manage it thanks to microbes in their gut.

q: Which stomach enzyme starts digesting the protein in dal and paneer?
note: It works best in the strongly acidic conditions of the stomach.

q: Table sugar, sucrose, splits into glucose and which other simple sugar?
Lemon juice added to chashni splits sucrose so the syrup won't crystallise. What is the result called?
note: The split sugars get in the way of sucrose crystals forming.

q: Heavy salting and sugaring both preserve food by drawing water out of microbes. What is this process called?
note: Water moves across cell membranes toward the saltier or sweeter side.

q: Why do dried fruits like anjeer and kishmish keep for months without a fridge?
a: They hold too little water for microbes
options: They hold too little water for microbes
They are too sweet to digest

q: Which French confectioner won a government prize for preserving food in heated, sealed containers?
note: His method came decades before anyone knew microbes caused spoilage.

q: What Japanese-named fifth basic taste describes a savoury, brothy flavour?
Which Japanese chemist found in 1908 that the savoury taste of kombu broth comes from glutamate?
note: He patented a seasoning made from it, launched as Ajinomoto in 1909.

q: How does the US FDA classify MSG as a food ingredient?
note: Its glutamate is the same as the glutamate found naturally in many foods.

q: A pinch of salt is known to tone down which taste in foods like karela?
note: Salt dampens how strongly the tongue registers bitter compounds.

q: Which stimulant is found in both chai and filter kaapi?
note: By dry weight, tea leaves hold more of it than roasted beans, but a cup holds less.

q: Which bitter stimulant in cocoa is dangerous to dogs because they break it down slowly?
note: Its name comes from the cocoa tree's Latin name, meaning 'food of the gods'.

q: The dry, puckering feel of strong black tea comes from which compounds?
Green and black tea come from the same plant. What happens to black tea's leaves?
note: Green tea leaves are heated soon after picking to stop this process.

q: Which amino acid, found mainly in tea leaves, adds a savoury note to green tea?
note: Shade-grown teas like matcha tend to be rich in it.

q: Why does a warm bottle of soda go flat faster than a cold one?
a: Gases dissolve less in warm liquids
options: Warmth turns the gas into water
Gases dissolve less in warm liquids

q: Fizzy soda tastes slightly tangy because its dissolved gas forms which weak acid?
note: The same acid forms when rainwater absorbs gas from the air.

q: Which acid gives most colas their sharp tang?
note: It appears as INS 338 on Indian ingredient labels.

q: Which plant hormone gas makes fruit ripen and spreads from ripe fruit to its neighbours?
note: A closed paper bag traps it and speeds up ripening.

q: FSSAI bans ripening mangoes with which chemical that releases acetylene gas?
note: FSSAI warns that its impurities can be harmful to health.

q: Which of these fruits does NOT keep ripening after it is picked?
note: Fruits that do ripen after picking are called climacteric.

q: Frying an egg turns its clear part white because heat does what to its proteins?
note: The proteins unfold and tangle, trapping water and scattering light.

q: Why does an old egg float in a bowl of water?
note: Moisture escapes through thousands of tiny pores in the shell over time.

q: Does a brown-shelled egg differ nutritionally from a white one?
a: No, shell colour depends on the hen's breed
options: No, shell colour depends on the hen's breed
Only brown eggs come from free-range hens
Yes, brown eggs have more protein
note: The USDA says shell colour doesn't affect quality, flavour or nutrients.

q: A deeper orange egg yolk mainly reflects what?
note: Feeds rich in yellow-orange plant pigments give darker yolks.

q: Why is a very fresh boiled egg often harder to peel than a week-old one?
a: Its white has a lower pH and clings to the membrane
options: Its white has a lower pH and clings to the membrane
note: As eggs age, the white slowly becomes more alkaline and lets go of the membrane.

q: Why do many cooks rinse rice before cooking it?
a: To wash off loose surface starch
options: To wash off loose surface starch
note: Less loose starch means fluffier, less sticky grains.

q: Starch granules soaking up water and swelling when heated is called what?
note: It is why sooji and cornflour thicken liquids as they cook.

q: Raw potatoes stored at fridge temperature for weeks build up more of what?
Green patches on potato skin can signal which natural toxin?
note: The green colour develops when potatoes are exposed to light.

q: Which chemical can form when starchy foods like chips and toast are fried, roasted or baked at high heat?
note: It forms from natural sugars and an amino acid called asparagine.

q: Which group of pigments gives beetroot its deep red-purple colour?
note: They can harmlessly turn some people's urine pink, an effect called beeturia.

q: Which pigments give jamun and brinjal skin their deep purple colour?
note: They change colour with acidity, turning redder in acid.

q: Which red pigment colours watermelon flesh and ripe tamatar?
Which is the oldest artificial sweetener, discovered by accident in 1879?
note: A chemist noticed a sweet taste on his hands at dinner after lab work.

q: Which zero-calorie sweetener is extracted from the leaves of a South American plant?
note: Its sweet compounds, steviol glycosides, are far sweeter than sugar.

q: Diet drinks carry a warning for phenylketonurics because aspartame breaks down into which amino acid?
note: People with PKU cannot break this amino acid down properly.

q: Which sugar alcohol, sometimes sold as 'birch sugar', is common in sugar-free chewing gum?
Which West African berry makes sour foods like lemons taste sweet for a while?
note: Its protein, miraculin, binds to sweet receptors and switches them on in acid.

q: Besides taste, which sense provides most of what we call a food's flavour?
note: That's why food seems bland when a cold blocks your nose.

q: Kulfi makers pack the moulds in ice mixed with salt. Why?
a: Salt makes the ice mixture colder than 0°C
options: Salt stops the kulfi melting later
Salt makes the ice mixture colder than 0°C
Salt keeps the ice from floating
note: Salt lowers the melting point, so the ice melts while pulling heat away.

q: Kulfi is denser than ice cream mainly because it is not what?
note: Ice cream can be up to half air by volume.

q: Water droplets skating and hissing on a very hot dosa tawa show which effect?
note: A cushion of vapour lifts each drop so it barely touches the metal.

q: Seasoning a cast-iron kadhai builds up a coating of what?
a: Oil bonded into a hard polymer
options: Oil bonded into a hard polymer
note: Each heated layer of oil adds to the natural non-stick surface.

q: Raw papaya is used in kebab marinades because of which meat-tenderising enzyme?
note: It breaks down tough proteins, the same job it does in tenderiser powders.

q: Haldi powder is made from which part of the haldi plant?
note: The underground stems are boiled, dried and ground.

q: Dry-roasting jeera deepens its aroma mainly by doing what?
a: Releasing volatile oils and browning the seeds
options: Releasing volatile oils and browning the seeds

q: Cooked rice left warm for hours can grow which spore-forming bacterium?
note: Its spores survive cooking, so food agencies advise cooling rice quickly.

q: A phulka puffs up on an open flame because of what?
note: The two thin layers separate as the moisture between them turns to steam.

q: The bubbles that fizz when pakoras hit hot oil are mostly what?
note: Oil doesn't boil at frying temperatures; the water in the batter does.

q: Which Polish biochemist coined the word 'vitamine' in 1912?
note: He thought they were all 'vital amines'; the final 'e' was dropped later.

q: Which American pioneered quick-frozen food after seeing Inuit fish freeze almost instantly in Labrador?
note: Fast freezing makes smaller ice crystals, which damage food texture less.

q: Which French physicist built the 'steam digester', forerunner of the pressure cooker, in 1679?
note: His design included an early safety valve to stop it bursting.

q: Why do limp vegetables crisp up again in cold water?
a: Their cells take water back in
options: Their cells take water back in

q: Why won't cooking oil mix with water?
note: Oil also floats because it is less dense than water.

q: Which natural fibre in fruit makes jams set into a gel?
note: Setting also needs the right amount of sugar and acid.

q: What are the dry, greyish patches on food left too long in a freezer called?
note: Airtight wrapping helps prevent it.

q: FSSAI's '+F' logo on packs of rice, oil or salt means the food is what?
What is the cooking liquid from chickpeas, which can be whipped into an egg-free foam, called?
note: The name blends the Latin words for water and bean.

q: Which word describes salt and sugar's tendency to soak up moisture from the air and clump?
note: Anti-caking agents are added to table salt to fight this.

q: Nimbu juice has a pH of roughly what?
note: Each step down the pH scale means ten times more acidic.

q: Which acid gives nimbu most of its sourness?
Imli's sourness comes mainly from which acid?
Which preservative, INS 211 on Indian labels, is common in ketchups and squashes?
note: It works best in acidic foods.

q: What is the international symbol that marks irradiated food called?
note: US rules require it on food that has been irradiated.

q: Which international food standards code is run jointly by the FAO and WHO?
note: Its name is Latin for 'food code'.

q: World Food Safety Day is marked every year on which date?
note: It was first observed in 2019.

q: Watermelon is roughly what percentage water?
Cocoa butter melts just below which temperature, so a good bar melts on the tongue?
Which compound replaces part of the regular namak in 'lite' salt blends?
Maida is wheat flour with which parts of the grain removed?
note: What remains is the starchy endosperm, milled very fine.

q: Which instrument checks milk's purity by measuring its density, revealing added water?
note: Watered-down milk is less dense, so the device sinks deeper in it.
